content:
Joint pain is not always arthritis. Short-lived pain after overuse or a minor injury usually settles in a few weeks with rest, gentle movement and simple painkillers. Pain that lasts longer, comes with swelling or long morning stiffness, or affects several joints may be arthritis and is worth discussing with your GP. A single hot, red, swollen joint with fever needs urgent help.

Common causes of joint pain

  • Strains, sprains and overuse, for example after gardening, sport or a new activity
  • Osteoarthritis, the most common type of arthritis, usually in knees, hips, hands and the spine, mainly after 45
  • Inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis, where the immune system attacks the joints
  • Gout, causing sudden severe pain, often in the big toe
  • Bursitis and tendinopathy, irritation of the cushioning sacs or tendons around a joint
  • Viral infections, which can cause temporary aches in several joints
  • Joint hypermobility, where joints move further than usual
  • Fibromyalgia, which causes widespread pain that is felt in and around joints

Clues that it might be osteoarthritis

  • you are over 45
  • pain is worse with activity and eases with rest
  • any morning stiffness lasts less than 30 minutes
  • one or a few large joints are affected, or the finger joints nearest the nails

NICE (NG226) says osteoarthritis can usually be diagnosed from symptoms alone, without an X-ray, in people who fit this picture.

Clues that it might be inflammatory arthritis

  • swelling in the joints, particularly the small joints of the hands and feet
  • stiffness for more than 30 minutes in the morning
  • pain that is worse after rest and better with movement
  • several joints affected, often on both sides of the body
  • tiredness, feeling generally unwell or weight loss
  • psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease or a family history of these conditions

NICE (NG100) recommends that people with persistent joint swelling are referred urgently to a rheumatologist, even if blood tests are normal.

Self-care for joint pain

For mild pain that has not lasted long:

  • keep moving gently. Rest the joint for a day or two if very sore, then build activity back up.
  • use an ice pack wrapped in a towel for swelling, or heat for stiffness
  • try simple painkillers or a topical anti-inflammatory gel. Ask your pharmacist what is suitable for you.
  • wear supportive shoes and pace demanding tasks
  • if you are overweight, losing some weight reduces strain on knees and hips

When to see your GP

  • pain has not improved after two weeks of self-care
  • you have swelling, warmth or stiffness that lasts for more than 30 minutes in the morning
  • several joints are painful or swollen
  • pain is stopping you working, sleeping or doing everyday tasks
  • you have other symptoms, such as rashes, mouth ulcers, dry eyes, or a change in bowel habits

Many areas let you self-refer to NHS physiotherapy for joint pain, which can be quicker than waiting for a GP appointment.

What your GP may do

Your GP will ask about your symptoms and examine the joints. Depending on what they find, they may arrange blood tests to check for inflammation and rheumatoid factor, X-rays, or a referral to physiotherapy or rheumatology. Bring a list of which joints hurt, when they are worst and anything that helps.

Keeping a symptom diary

Noting your pain levels, stiffness and any swelling each day for a week or two can help you and your GP spot patterns. Take photos of any swelling, as it may go down before your appointment.

Remember that most joint pain is not serious and many causes improve with time and the right self-care. Getting checked early, though, means that if it is arthritis you can start the right treatment sooner.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
